title: Healthcare & Patient Care Foundations
tagline: Vital signs, infection control, first aid and CPR, safe medication practice, and how healthcare works in Dubai.

superpower.name: First Responder
superpower.description: Knows what to do when someone is unwell: better wellbeing and more from care jobs.

syllabus: Week 1: How healthcare works in Dubai, and the caring professional
Week 2: Vital signs and observing patients
Week 3: Infection control and safe medication
Week 4: First aid, CPR and emergencies

weeks.title: Healthcare in Dubai
weeks.objective: Understand the system, the regulators and what it means to care professionally.

slides.title: The System and Its Regulators
slides.body: Healthcare in Dubai is regulated by the Dubai Health Authority (DHA). Doctors, nurses and allied health workers must be licensed by DHA (through its Sheryan system) before they can practise, usually after passing a licensing exam. Health insurance is mandatory for residents in Dubai.
bullets: DHA licenses professionals and facilities in Dubai
Licensing exams and verified qualifications come before practice
Health insurance is compulsory for Dubai residents, usually provided by the employer
Emergency departments treat emergencies regardless of insurance
slides.takeaway: In Dubai, you need a DHA licence to practise: qualifications alone aren't enough.

slides.title: The Caring Professional
slides.body: Patients remember how they were treated. Professional care combines skill with dignity, privacy and clear communication, often across many languages and cultures.
bullets: Consent: explain and ask before any care
Confidentiality: patient information is shared only with those who need it
Dignity and cultural respect: same-gender carers where requested
Clear handovers: the SBAR method (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
slides.takeaway: Skill keeps patients safe; kindness makes them feel safe.

lab.title: SBAR Handover Lab
lab.brief: Write an SBAR handover for a patient whose breathing has worsened during your shift.
lab.proTip: Lead with the most important fact: what's wrong right now.

caseStudy.scenario: A patient's relative phones the ward asking for their test results. What do you do?

options.text: Read the results out to be helpful.
Politely explain you can't share information without the patient's consent, and offer to pass on a message.
options.explanation: Confidentiality protects patients; consent comes first.
Be polite and helpful within the rules.

quiz.question: Who licenses healthcare professionals in Dubai?
quiz.explanation: The DHA licenses professionals and facilities.

weeks.title: Vital Signs
weeks.objective: Measure and interpret the basic signs of health and spot a patient getting worse.

slides.title: Normal Adult Ranges
slides.body: Vital signs are the quickest picture of how a patient is doing. Know the normal adult ranges so you notice when something is off.
bullets: Heart rate: 60 to 100 beats per minute
Breathing rate: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
Blood pressure: around 120/80 mmHg or lower
Temperature: about 36.1 to 37.2°C
Oxygen saturation (SpO2): 95 to 100% for most healthy adults
slides.takeaway: Know normal, so you can spot abnormal.

slides.title: Spotting Deterioration
slides.body: A patient rarely gets worse without warning. Breathing rate is often the first sign to change, and early warning scores add up small changes into a clear alarm.
bullets: Rising breathing rate, falling SpO2, falling blood pressure, rising heart rate
New confusion or drowsiness is a red flag
Repeat observations and record them on a chart
Escalate early: tell the nurse in charge or doctor straight away
slides.example:
A patient's observations at 2pm and 4pm:
• Breathing: 16, then 26 a minute
• Heart rate: 82, then 112
• SpO2: 97%, then 91%
• New confusion at 4pm
Every sign is moving the wrong way: escalate now, using SBAR.
slides.takeaway: Trends matter more than one reading: chart them and escalate early.

lab.title: Observations Lab
lab.brief: Take and chart a full set of observations on a classmate twice, 30 minutes apart, and note anything outside the normal range.
lab.proTip: Count breathing for a full 30 seconds without telling the person: they breathe differently when watched.

caseStudy.scenario: A patient's breathing rate rises from 14 to 28 over an hour, and they seem confused. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the next routine check in 4 hours.
options.explanation: These are signs of serious deterioration.

options.text: Escalate immediately to the nurse in charge or doctor, with your observations.
Give them a glass of water.

weeks.title: Infection Control and Medication Safety
weeks.objective: Stop infections spreading and give medicines safely.

slides.title: Hand Hygiene and PPE
slides.body: Clean hands are the single most effective way to prevent infections in healthcare. The WHO's 'five moments' define exactly when.
bullets: Before touching a patient
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After exposure to body fluids
After touching a patient
After touching the patient's surroundings
PPE on: gown, mask, goggles, gloves. Off: gloves, goggles, gown, mask, then wash hands
slides.takeaway: Clean hands save more lives than any machine in the hospital.

slides.title: Giving Medicines Safely
slides.body: Medication errors are among the most common harms in healthcare. Every dose is checked against the five rights, and anything unclear is questioned before it's given.
bullets: Right patient: check two identifiers (name and date of birth)
Right drug
Right dose
Right route (by mouth, injection…)
Right time
Check allergies first; record every dose immediately
slides.example:
A doctor prescribes 500 mg of a medicine, and the tablets are 250 mg each.
Dose ÷ strength = 500 ÷ 250 = 2 tablets.
Before giving them: check the patient's name and date of birth, allergies, route and time, then record it.
slides.takeaway: If any of the five rights is uncertain, stop and check.

lab.title: Infection Control Lab
lab.brief: Demonstrate handwashing (40 to 60 seconds) and putting on and taking off PPE in the right order.
lab.deliverable: A checklist signed by a peer.
lab.proTip: Taking PPE off is where contamination happens: go slowly.

caseStudy.scenario: You're about to give a tablet and the patient says 'I'm allergic to that.' The chart shows no allergy. What do you do?

options.text: Give it; the chart is correct.
options.explanation: Never ignore a patient's report of allergy.

options.text: Hold the dose, check with the prescriber, and update the allergy record if confirmed.
options.explanation: Stop, check and record: patient safety first.
A smaller dose can still cause a reaction.

quiz.question: How many 'moments' of hand hygiene does the WHO define?
Prescribed 1,000 mg; tablets are 500 mg. How many?

weeks.title: First Aid, CPR and Emergencies
weeks.objective: Act in the first minutes, when it matters most.

slides.title: Emergency Basics in the UAE
slides.body: In an emergency, every minute counts. Make sure the scene is safe, call for help early, and start first aid.
bullets: Ambulance: 998. Police: 999. Fire: 997
Danger, Response, Shout for help, Airway, Breathing (DRSAB)
Recovery position for someone unconscious but breathing normally
Severe bleeding: firm direct pressure
slides.takeaway: Call early, act fast: the first minutes decide the outcome.

slides.title: CPR for Adults
slides.body: If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR immediately and get a defibrillator (AED). Hands-only CPR is far better than nothing.
bullets: Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: 100 to 120 compressions a minute
Depth: 5 to 6 cm for an adult, letting the chest fully rise
If trained: 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths
Use an AED as soon as it arrives and follow its voice instructions
slides.takeaway: Good, continuous compressions keep blood flowing to the brain until help arrives.

lab.title: First Aid Scenario Lab
lab.brief: Run three scenarios on a manikin: an unconscious breathing adult, an adult in cardiac arrest, and severe bleeding.
lab.deliverable: A record of the actions and their order.
lab.proTip: Compressions to the beat of a 100 to 120 bpm song help keep the right pace.

caseStudy.scenario: At a mall, a man collapses and isn't breathing normally. A bystander is filming. What's first?

options.text: Wait for the ambulance before doing anything.
options.explanation: Without CPR the chance of survival falls fast.

options.text: Call 998 (or tell someone to), start CPR, and ask someone to bring the nearest AED.
options.explanation: Call, compress, and get an AED: the chain of survival.
Never give an unresponsive person anything by mouth.
